GlucoCraft Panel Added
The wall panel **Panel A** (480 × 480, square) is connected to GlucoCraft.

GlucoCraft's dashboard is set to show the rectangular display card (800 × 480), which does not match the shape of this panel. The display card on the dashboard is chosen independently of the panels: Settings > Devices & services > GlucoCraft > Configure > Display card and wall panels > *Display card layout*. The square card matches square panels, such as the 480 × 480 example panel; the rectangular card matches 800 × 480 panels and is close to rectangular panels of other sizes, such as the 1024 × 600 and 480 × 320 example panels. A card that does not match a panel shows the same information in a different layout.

phone.panel_address|none: no wall-panel address has been created. The box *Create a new wall-panel address* below creates it; it is needed before the first wall panel is built, because the build needs its id. Only the wall panels use it.
phone.panel_address|set: the address of the wall panels' data is `http://<Home Assistant address>/api/webhook/glucocraft_panel_0123?file=backfill` (and `?file=delta`). Its id, `glucocraft_panel_0123`, goes into the panel's secrets.yaml. The address is read-only and answers only on the home network; it is protected by its id and by Home Assistant's check that a request comes from the local network. This check works only when Home Assistant sees each panel's own network address; behind a reverse proxy, the proxy and Home Assistant must be set up to pass it on. The panels download their data from this address over plain HTTP, which is not encrypted: other devices on the same network could read the data or, by posing as Home Assistant, send false data to a panel; the panels' downloaded data are therefore only as private as the home network. After a log, backup or screenshot containing the address was shared, a new address can be created below.

5 40.0 351.6 8b l This report: 
5 86.7 351.6 8 l The CGM Report shows the standardized metrics and glucose profile recommended for the Ambulatory Glucose Profile (Battelino et al.,
5 40.0 341.0 8 l 2019; Bergenstal et al., 2013). GlucoCraft is not affiliated with or endorsed by the cited authors or any CGM manufacturer. The values are calculated

5 40.0 316.9 8b l Summary and full report: 
5 137.3 316.9 8 l The 2019 international consensus describes a single-page report as of value and states that more detailed reports, for
5 40.0 306.3 8 l example detailed daily reports, "should remain available for individualized review" (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data Presentation
5 40.0 295.8 8 l section, para. 2). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care recommend a minimum of a single-page report, such as the
5 40.0 285.2 8 l standardized CGM report and a weekly summary, and state that options for daily and weekly reports and raw data should be available (American
5 40.0 274.7 8 l Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026b, Recommendation 7.9). This explains why the CGM Report has a
5 40.0 264.1 8 l summary and a full report with daily profiles, a daily summary and an hourly log, and why the readings can be exported as comma-separated values
5 40.0 253.5 8 l (CSV). The summary contains the 14-day section (time in ranges, glucose metrics, the glucose profile and the daily glucose profiles), the
5 40.0 243.0 8 l longer-term overview (30 days and longer), the weekly trend (90 days and 6 months), Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, the comparison with the
5 40.0 232.4 8 l previous period (not in the 6-month report), Data Quality and Laboratory A1C. The full report adds Hypoglycemia Events by Period, the daily
5 40.0 221.9 8 l glucose profiles of the whole period (30 days and longer), Daily Patterns, the Daily Summary, the Daily Log (one row per day, one column per hour)
5 40.0 211.3 8 l and the Monthly Summary (every calendar month of the period). The two appendices are added to either form only when chosen. Each section
5 40.0 200.7 8 l opens with a caption line that names its rule and source, shows its data and ends with Notes that explain them with their sources.
5 40.0 187.2 8b l Targets and assessments: 
5 142.7 187.2 8 l GlucoCraft sets no targets or ranges and makes no assessments. Every target and range shown is either taken from the
5 40.0 176.6 8 l cited published sources (consensus statements, studies and manufacturer documentation), each named as what it is — consensus: ranges and
5 40.0 166.1 8 l targets (Battelino et al., 2019), tight range (Battelino et al., 2023), CV (Battelino et al., 2019; the study by Monnier et al., 2017); studies: GMI
5 40.0 155.5 8 l (Bergenstal et al., 2018), GRI (Klonoff et al., 2023) — or set by the user in GlucoCraft's settings. Where GlucoCraft applies a rule of its own (for
5 40.0 144.9 8 l example the length of a data gap, or the zone of a GRI value), it is labeled as a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft is designed to calculate and display; it
5 40.0 134.4 8 l sends notifications, prints reports and saves PDF and CSV files only as chosen in its settings or requested by the user. Where colors or the words
5 40.0 123.8 8 l met / not met appear, they are arithmetic comparisons with the cited target or the custom goal, not clinical assessments.

6 62.2 691.3 8 l time without CGM data is excluded from all values. A data gap is an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three
6 40.0 680.8 8 l reading intervals, whichever is longer, the reading interval being the median of the 10 intervals before the reading (the higher of the two middle values;
6 40.0 670.2 8 l filled with the intervals after it at the start of the data; the usual interval of the source with fewer than 3). Each reading represents the time until the
6 40.0 659.6 8 l next reading, so a shorter dropout counts in full (the values in between are not known); before a gap, only its own reading interval. Sensor active is
6 40.0 649.1 8 l that time as a share of the period; the CGM system's own figure also counts readings not received for this report (for example during delivery or
6 40.0 638.5 8 l network outages) and applies its own rules to short dropouts. Every percentage and every statistic weights each reading by the time it represents.
6 40.0 628.0 8 l This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
6 40.0 614.4 8b l Readings at the sensor's limit: 
6 157.9 614.4 8 l a reading outside the CGM sensor's measurement range (shown in this report as LO or HI) has no value: it is left out
6 40.0 603.8 8 l of the mean, the standard deviation, the CV, the GMI, the lowest and highest values and the glucose curves, and it is counted as very low or very
6 40.0 593.3 8 l high in the time in ranges and in the events, where an event's lowest value can be LO. Its number and time are noted under the statistics. No
6 40.0 582.7 8 l consensus document addresses such readings, and other software treats them differently: the report software of Abbott Diabetes Care shows them
6 40.0 572.2 8 l at the limit (Abbott Diabetes Care, 2018, p. 7), so the values can differ from a manufacturer's report. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

10 40.0 775.9 8b l Summary and full report: 
10 137.3 775.9 8 l The 2019 international consensus describes a single-page report as of value and states that more detailed reports, for
10 40.0 765.3 8 l example detailed daily reports, "should remain available for individualized review" (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data
10 40.0 754.8 8 l Presentation section, para. 2). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care recommend a minimum of a single-page report,
10 40.0 744.2 8 l such as the standardized CGM report and a weekly summary, and state that options for daily and weekly reports and raw data should be
10 40.0 733.6 8 l available (American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026b, Recommendation 7.9). This explains why the
10 40.0 723.1 8 l CGM Report has a summary and a full report with daily profiles, a daily summary and an hourly log, and why the readings can be exported as
10 40.0 712.5 8 l comma-separated values (CSV). The summary contains the 14-day section (time in ranges, glucose metrics, the glucose profile and the daily
10 40.0 702.0 8 l glucose profiles), the longer-term overview (30 days and longer), the weekly trend (90 days and 6 months), Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, the
10 40.0 691.4 8 l comparison with the previous period (not in the 6-month report), Data Quality and Laboratory A1C. The full report adds Hypoglycemia Events
10 40.0 680.8 8 l by Period, the daily glucose profiles of the whole period (30 days and longer), Daily Patterns, the Daily Summary, the Daily Log (one row per
10 40.0 670.3 8 l day, one column per hour) and the Monthly Summary (every calendar month of the period). The two appendices are added to either form only
10 40.0 659.7 8 l when chosen. Each section opens with a caption line that names its rule and source, shows its data and ends with Notes that explain them with
10 40.0 649.2 8 l their sources.
10 40.0 635.6 8b l Targets and assessments: 
10 142.7 635.6 8 l GlucoCraft sets no targets or ranges and makes no assessments. Every target and range shown is either taken from
10 40.0 625.0 8 l the cited published sources (consensus statements, studies and manufacturer documentation), each named as what it is — consensus: ranges
10 40.0 614.5 8 l and targets (Battelino et al., 2019), tight range (Battelino et al., 2023), CV (Battelino et al., 2019; the study by Monnier et al., 2017); studies:
10 40.0 603.9 8 l GMI (Bergenstal et al., 2018), GRI (Klonoff et al., 2023) — or set by the user in GlucoCraft's settings. Where GlucoCraft applies a rule of its own
10 40.0 593.4 8 l (for example the length of a data gap, or the zone of a GRI value), it is labeled as a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft is designed to calculate and
10 40.0 582.8 8 l display; it sends notifications, prints reports and saves PDF and CSV files only as chosen in its settings or requested by the user. Where colors
10 40.0 572.2 8 l or the words met / not met appear, they are arithmetic comparisons with the cited target or the custom goal, not clinical assessments.

10 90.2 558.7 8 l Test source.
10 40.0 545.1 8b l Report period: 
10 97.3 545.1 8 l full days ending at midnight before the report was created; the days and the night and day periods follow the time zone of the
10 40.0 534.6 8 l system that created the report. The first section always shows the most recent 14 days, the recommended period (Battelino et al., 2019;
10 40.0 524.0 8 l Bergenstal et al., 2013).
10 40.0 510.4 8b l Period length: 
10 96.0 510.4 8 l Among 257 people with type 1 diabetes, 14 days of CGM data estimated the 3-month time in range and mean glucose closely
10 40.0 499.9 8 l (Riddlesworth et al., 2018). Time below range is less precise: among 329 people with type 1 diabetes with 90 days of CGM data, its error
10 40.0 489.3 8 l roughly halved from 10 to 30 days of data and continued to decrease to 60 days (Cichosz et al., 2023).
10 40.0 475.8 8b l Data: 
10 62.2 475.8 8 l time without CGM data is excluded from all values. A data gap is an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three
10 40.0 465.2 8 l reading intervals, whichever is longer, the reading interval being the median of the 10 intervals before the reading (the higher of the two middle
10 40.0 454.6 8 l values; filled with the intervals after it at the start of the data; the usual interval of the source with fewer than 3). Each reading represents the time
10 40.0 444.1 8 l until the next reading, so a shorter dropout counts in full (the values in between are not known); before a gap, only its own reading interval.
10 40.0 433.5 8 l Sensor active is that time as a share of the period; the CGM system's own figure also counts readings not received for this report (for example
10 40.0 423.0 8 l during delivery or network outages) and applies its own rules to short dropouts. Every percentage and every statistic weights each reading by the
10 40.0 412.4 8 l time it represents. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
10 40.0 398.8 8b l Readings at the sensor's limit: 
10 157.9 398.8 8 l a reading outside the CGM sensor's measurement range (shown in this report as LO or HI) has no value: it is
10 40.0 388.3 8 l left out of the mean, the standard deviation, the CV, the GMI, the lowest and highest values and the glucose curves, and it is counted as very
10 40.0 377.7 8 l low or very high in the time in ranges and in the events, where an event's lowest value can be LO. Its number and time are noted under the
10 40.0 367.2 8 l statistics. No consensus document addresses such readings, and other software treats them differently: the report software of Abbott Diabetes
10 40.0 356.6 8 l Care shows them at the limit (Abbott Diabetes Care, 2018, p. 7), so the values can differ from a manufacturer's report. This method is a
10 40.0 346.0 8 l GlucoCraft rule.
10 40.0 332.5 8b l Enough data: 
10 93.3 332.5 8 l the values of a period (time in ranges, mean glucose, SD, CV, GMI, GRI, lowest and highest value, events and comparisons, also
10 40.0 321.9 8 l those of a week or a day) are shown only when its sensor active is at least 70%, compared before rounding; otherwise the period's sensor active
10 40.0 311.4 8 l is given and a dash (-) stands in place of its values. The 70% condition is published for 14-day periods (Battelino et al., 2019, Table 2); this
10 40.0 300.8 8 l report applies it to periods of every length. The glucose profiles and the Daily Log show the readings received in any case. This method is a
10 40.0 290.2 8 l GlucoCraft rule. A dash (-) also marks a value that does not exist for a period, such as GMI for fewer than 14 days.
10 40.0 276.7 8b l Rounding: 
10 82.2 276.7 8 l every value is calculated from the readings as stored and rounded once, where it is shown: percentages to one decimal (two where
10 40.0 266.1 8 l one decimal would show a target's value that the value does not meet), glucose in mg/dL to whole numbers and in mmol/L to one decimal, with
10 40.0 255.6 8 l halves rounded away from zero. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

11 40.0 406.5 8b l Definition. 
11 81.3 406.5 8 l An event is a period in which sensor glucose stays above 13,9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL) for at least 120 minutes. It ends when glucose
11 40.0 396.0 8 l has returned to 10,0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) or below for 15 minutes (Battelino et al., 2023, p. 48). This definition was made for counting events in
11 40.0 385.4 8 l clinical trials: the 2023 international consensus statement lists the "extended hyperglycaemic event rate" as a secondary endpoint for clinical
11 40.0 374.9 8 l studies (Battelino et al., 2023, p. 48). The same statement also describes extended hyperglycemia as 90 cumulative minutes above 13,9 mmol/L
11 40.0 364.3 8 l (250 mg/dL) within a 120-minute period (Battelino et al., 2023, Table 4); this report uses the version that states both a start and an end.
11 40.0 350.7 8b l No clinical-care standard. 
11 139.6 350.7 8 l The clinical-care consensus describes high glucose by the time above 10,0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) and above 13,9
11 40.0 340.2 8 l mmol/L (250 mg/dL) and sets targets for those times (Battelino et al., 2019); the ADA Standards of Care do the same (American Diabetes
11 40.0 329.6 8 l Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026a, Table 6.2). Neither defines high-glucose events or a target for their number.
11 40.0 319.1 8 l The 2023 definition exists only for research, so the count has no published target and no clinical interpretation.

11 70.7 305.5 8 l (GlucoCraft rules where the source does not specify):
11 40.0 291.9 8b l 1.
11 48.9 291.9 8 l The readings are the CGM values received for this report, in mg/dL; a HI reading counts at the sensor's upper limit (always above 250 mg/dL).
11 40.0 281.4 8 l The limits in mmol/L are 13,9 and 10,0.
11 40.0 267.8 8b l 2.
11 48.9 267.8 8 l Start: a run of consecutive readings, each above 250 mg/dL, becomes an event once the time it covers reaches 120 minutes. The time a run
11 40.0 257.3 8 l covers is measured as in all statistics of this report: each reading counts until the next reading, or for its own reading interval before a data gap.
11 40.0 246.7 8 l The event's start time is the time of the run's first reading.
11 40.0 233.1 8b l 3.
11 48.9 233.1 8 l During the event, readings from 181 to 250 mg/dL do not end it.
11 40.0 219.6 8b l 4.
11 48.9 219.6 8 l End: the event ends at the first reading of the first run of readings at or below 180 mg/dL that covers 15 minutes. Its duration is the time from its
11 40.0 209.0 8 l start to that reading.
11 40.0 195.5 8b l 5.
11 48.9 195.5 8 l Data gaps: a data gap (an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three reading intervals, whichever is longer) ends a
11 40.0 184.9 8 l running event at the end of its last reading before the gap, which counts for its own reading interval. A run above 250 mg/dL interrupted by a gap
11 40.0 174.3 8 l is an event only if it had already covered 120 minutes before the gap.
11 40.0 160.8 8b l 6.
11 48.9 160.8 8 l Counting: each event is counted once, in the period and on the day in which it starts, also when it continues past midnight. The appendix
11 40.0 150.2 8 l shows the number of events, their total duration and the longest event for the report period.

Other groups: 
The consensus also publishes different targets for some groups, such as older or high-risk adults and pregnancy (Battelino et al.,
2019, Tables 3 and 4). They are not included here. The results here are calculated with the ranges and targets for adults in general, not with the
ranges for these groups.
Names of the ranges: 
The 2019 international consensus names the glucose ranges of the standardized report "Very High" (level 2), "High" (level 1),
"Low" (level 1) and "Very Low" (level 2) (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data Presentation section, para. 1). This explains the range
names Very high, High, Low and Very low.
CV target: 
The 2019 international consensus sets the target for glycemic variability at a coefficient of variation (%CV) of 36% or less (Battelino et al.,
2019, Table 2), a value it takes from Monnier et al. (2017). The ADA Standards of Care list the same goal of 36% or less (American Diabetes
Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026a, Table 6.2). This explains the target in the CV row.
Metrics: 
mean glucose and the standard deviation (SD) are weighted by time, as described in About This Report (Data). Coefficient of variation (CV)
= SD ÷ mean glucose × 100 (Danne et al., 2017). Glucose management indicator (GMI) in percent = 3.31 + 0.02392 × mean glucose in mg/dL
(Bergenstal et al., 2018). Glycemia Risk Index (GRI) = 3.0 × very low + 2.4 × low + 1.6 × very high + 0.8 × high, each in percent of time, at most 100;
its hypoglycemia component is very low + 0.8 × low and its hyperglycemia component very high + 0.5 × high (Klonoff et al., 2023).
Glucose profile: 
The 2023 international consensus statement on CGM metrics for clinical trials describes four features of the graph of the glucose
profile: the target glucose range, the median line, the shaded 25th to 75th percentile band and the outer 5th to 95th percentile band (Battelino et al.,
2023, p. 49). This explains the lines and shaded bands of the glucose profile in the CGM Report. The cited sources do not describe the smoothing of
the profile; each 15-minute period is pooled with the two neighboring periods (45 minutes), and each reading counts once for every whole minute it
represents. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

Time below range by night and day, and the hypoglycemia events that began in the period (level 1: below 70 mg/dL; level 2: below 54 mg/dL). Level 2
events are also counted as level 1 events. Consensus targets for the whole period (Battelino et al., 2019).
The 2017 international consensus quantifies hypoglycemia both as the percentage of CGM values, or the minutes or hours, below a threshold and "as
the number of hypoglycemic events that occur over the given CGM reporting period" (Danne et al., 2017, Section 4, para. 13). This explains why this
section shows both the time below range and the number of events for the same period.
The 2017 international consensus states that "readings below the threshold for at least 15 min" are considered an event and that the event ends with
readings for 15 minutes at 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or higher (Danne et al., 2017, Section 4, para. 14). This explains how the level 1 and level 2 events
in the Hypoglycemia section are counted: an event is counted once its readings have been below its limit for 15 minutes, starts at its first reading
below the limit, and ends with 15 minutes at 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or higher.
Hypoglycemia event: 
An event is counted once its readings have been below its limit for 15 minutes, and it then starts at its first reading below the
limit. Its duration runs to the first reading of the 15 minutes at or above 70 mg/dL, or to the end of the time its last reading represents when a data
gap (as defined in About This Report, Data) follows or the readings end; it is counted in the period in which it starts, a level 2 event in that of its level
1 event. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. No consensus rule exists for these details.
Night and day: 
The 2017 international consensus reports the glucose metrics in three time blocks, sleep, wake and 24 hours, with default times from
midnight to 6 in the morning for sleep and from 6 in the morning to midnight for wake (Danne et al., 2017, Section 7). For clinical trials, the 2023

About This Report
For development and testing only. 
GlucoCraft is free, open-source software, made available for development and testing. It is not intended for any
medical purpose, including diagnosing, monitoring, treating or managing diabetes or any other medical condition, or for making treatment decisions.
It has not been cleared, approved or certified as a medical device by the FDA or any other regulator. Its information and notifications can be late,
missing or wrong. Its notifications are not alarms. GlucoCraft is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 only
(AGPL-3.0-only), and is provided without warranty and, as far as the law allows, without liability (sections 15 and 16 of the license).
This report: 
The CGM Report shows the standardized metrics and glucose profile recommended for the Ambulatory Glucose Profile (Battelino et al.,
2019; Bergenstal et al., 2013). GlucoCraft is not affiliated with or endorsed by the cited authors or any CGM manufacturer. The values are calculated
from the data received from the glucose sources and can differ from the reports of the CGM manufacturer's software.
Summary and full report: 
The 2019 international consensus describes a single-page report as of value and states that more detailed reports, for
example detailed daily reports, "should remain available for individualized review" (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data Presentation
section, para. 2). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care recommend a minimum of a single-page report, such as the
standardized CGM report and a weekly summary, and state that options for daily and weekly reports and raw data should be available (American
Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026b, Recommendation 7.9). This explains why the CGM Report has a
summary and a full report with daily profiles, a daily summary and an hourly log, and why the readings can be exported as comma-separated values
(CSV). The summary contains the 14-day section (time in ranges, glucose metrics, the glucose profile and the daily glucose profiles), the
longer-term overview (30 days and longer), the weekly trend (90 days and 6 months), Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, the comparison with the
previous period (not in the 6-month report), Data Quality and Laboratory A1C. The full report adds Hypoglycemia Events by Period, the daily
glucose profiles of the whole period (30 days and longer), Daily Patterns, the Daily Summary, the Daily Log (one row per day, one column per hour)
and the Monthly Summary (every calendar month of the period). The two appendices are added to either form only when chosen. Each section
opens with a caption line that names its rule and source, shows its data and ends with Notes that explain them with their sources.
Targets and assessments: 
GlucoCraft sets no targets or ranges and makes no assessments. Every target and range shown is either taken from the
cited published sources (consensus statements, studies and manufacturer documentation), each named as what it is — consensus: ranges and
targets (Battelino et al., 2019), tight range (Battelino et al., 2023), CV (Battelino et al., 2019; the study by Monnier et al., 2017); studies: GMI
(Bergenstal et al., 2018), GRI (Klonoff et al., 2023) — or set by the user in GlucoCraft's settings. Where GlucoCraft applies a rule of its own (for
example the length of a data gap, or the zone of a GRI value), it is labeled as a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft is designed to calculate and display; it
sends notifications, prints reports and saves PDF and CSV files only as chosen in its settings or requested by the user. Where colors or the words
met / not met appear, they are arithmetic comparisons with the cited target or the custom goal, not clinical assessments.

Period length: 
Among 257 people with type 1 diabetes, 14 days of CGM data estimated the 3-month time in range and mean glucose closely
(Riddlesworth et al., 2018). Time below range is less precise: among 329 people with type 1 diabetes with 90 days of CGM data, its error roughly
halved from 10 to 30 days of data and continued to decrease to 60 days (Cichosz et al., 2023).
Data: 
time without CGM data is excluded from all values. A data gap is an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three
reading intervals, whichever is longer, the reading interval being the median of the 10 intervals before the reading (the higher of the two middle values;
filled with the intervals after it at the start of the data; the usual interval of the source with fewer than 3). Each reading represents the time until the
next reading, so a shorter dropout counts in full (the values in between are not known); before a gap, only its own reading interval. Sensor active is
that time as a share of the period; the CGM system's own figure also counts readings not received for this report (for example during delivery or
network outages) and applies its own rules to short dropouts. Every percentage and every statistic weights each reading by the time it represents.
This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Readings at the sensor's limit: 
a reading outside the CGM sensor's measurement range (shown in this report as LO or HI) has no value: it is left out
of the mean, the standard deviation, the CV, the GMI, the lowest and highest values and the glucose curves, and it is counted as very low or very
high in the time in ranges and in the events, where an event's lowest value can be LO. Its number and time are noted under the statistics. No
consensus document addresses such readings, and other software treats them differently: the report software of Abbott Diabetes Care shows them
at the limit (Abbott Diabetes Care, 2018, p. 7), so the values can differ from a manufacturer's report. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Enough data: 
the values of a period (time in ranges, mean glucose, SD, CV, GMI, GRI, lowest and highest value, events and comparisons, also
those of a week or a day) are shown only when its sensor active is at least 70%, compared before rounding; otherwise the period's sensor active is
given and a dash (-) stands in place of its values. The 70% condition is published for 14-day periods (Battelino et al., 2019, Table 2); this report
applies it to periods of every length. The glucose profiles and the Daily Log show the readings received in any case. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
A dash (-) also marks a value that does not exist for a period, such as GMI for fewer than 14 days.
Rounding: 
every value is calculated from the readings as stored and rounded once, where it is shown: percentages to one decimal (two where one
decimal would show a target's value that the value does not meet), glucose in mg/dL to whole numbers and in mmol/L to one decimal, with halves
rounded away from zero. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Durations: 
d, days; h, hours; min, minutes.
Not included: 
food intake, insulin, physical activity and device information are not part of the data.

Names of the ranges: 
The 2019 international consensus names the glucose ranges of the standardized report "Very High" (level 2), "High" (level
1), "Low" (level 1) and "Very Low" (level 2) (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data Presentation section, para. 1). This explains the
range names Very high, High, Low and Very low.
CV target: 
The 2019 international consensus sets the target for glycemic variability at a coefficient of variation (%CV) of 36% or less (Battelino et
al., 2019, Table 2), a value it takes from Monnier et al. (2017). The ADA Standards of Care list the same goal of 36% or less (American Diabetes
Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026a, Table 6.2). This explains the target in the CV row.
Metrics: 
mean glucose and the standard deviation (SD) are weighted by time, as described in About This Report (Data). Coefficient of variation
(CV) = SD ÷ mean glucose × 100 (Danne et al., 2017). Glucose management indicator (GMI) in percent = 3,31 + 0,02392 × mean glucose in
mg/dL (Bergenstal et al., 2018). Glycemia Risk Index (GRI) = 3,0 × very low + 2,4 × low + 1,6 × very high + 0,8 × high, each in percent of time, at
most 100; its hypoglycemia component is very low + 0,8 × low and its hyperglycemia component very high + 0,5 × high (Klonoff et al., 2023).
Glucose profile: 
The 2023 international consensus statement on CGM metrics for clinical trials describes four features of the graph of the
glucose profile: the target glucose range, the median line, the shaded 25th to 75th percentile band and the outer 5th to 95th percentile band
(Battelino et al., 2023, p. 49). This explains the lines and shaded bands of the glucose profile in the CGM Report. The cited sources do not
describe the smoothing of the profile; each 15-minute period is pooled with the two neighboring periods (45 minutes), and each reading counts
once for every whole minute it represents. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

Level 2 events are also counted as level 1 events. Consensus targets for the whole period (Battelino et al., 2019).
The 2017 international consensus quantifies hypoglycemia both as the percentage of CGM values, or the minutes or hours, below a threshold
and "as the number of hypoglycemic events that occur over the given CGM reporting period" (Danne et al., 2017, Section 4, para. 13). This
explains why this section shows both the time below range and the number of events for the same period.
The 2017 international consensus states that "readings below the threshold for at least 15 min" are considered an event and that the event ends
with readings for 15 minutes at 3,9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) or higher (Danne et al., 2017, Section 4, para. 14). This explains how the level 1 and level
2 events in the Hypoglycemia section are counted: an event is counted once its readings have been below its limit for 15 minutes, starts at its first
reading below the limit, and ends with 15 minutes at 3,9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) or higher.
Hypoglycemia event: 
An event is counted once its readings have been below its limit for 15 minutes, and it then starts at its first reading below
the limit. Its duration runs to the first reading of the 15 minutes at or above 3,9 mmol/L, or to the end of the time its last reading represents when
a data gap (as defined in About This Report, Data) follows or the readings end; it is counted in the period in which it starts, a level 2 event in that
of its level 1 event. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. No consensus rule exists for these details.
Night and day: 
The 2017 international consensus reports the glucose metrics in three time blocks, sleep, wake and 24 hours, with default times
from midnight to 6 in the morning for sleep and from 6 in the morning to midnight for wake (Danne et al., 2017, Section 7). For clinical trials, the
2023 international consensus statement reports nocturnal data for 00:00 to 05:59 and daytime data for 06:00 to 23:59 (Battelino et al., 2023,
Panel 2). This explains the Night (00:00–05:59) and Day (06:00–23:59) columns of the Hypoglycemia table; the report's night is a clock period,
not a measure of sleep.
Chart: 
Each marker is one level 1 event, at its start time and lowest value; the marker size increases with the duration, up to 120 minutes. The
darker markers are events that contain a level 2 event (at least 15 consecutive minutes below 3,0 mmol/L; Danne et al., 2017, Section 4). The
solid line marks 3,9 mmol/L and the broken line 3,0 mmol/L. A lowest value below the CGM sensor's measurement range (LO) is drawn at the
sensor's lower limit.

Close to, but not the same as, the CGM system's own figure: only the readings received are counted. The American Diabetes Association (ADA)
Standards of Care list two conditions for valid CGM data: at least 14 days of wear, and the CGM active for 70% of the time over those 14 days
(American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026a, Table 6.2). The 2019 international consensus gives the
same 14 days and 70%, counted as a share of the possible CGM readings (Battelino et al., 2019, Table 2). For this reason, the values of a period
are shown only with at least 70% sensor active, GMI and GRI only for periods of 14 days or more, each section notes a period with less, and the
custom appendix compares a custom goal (met / not met) only for periods that meet both conditions. Sensor active is measured as the share of
the period represented by the readings received. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
A new sensor is detected when the stated sensor expiry (where one is provided) moves more than a day later, or when the source reports the
warm-up marker that some CGM systems send; the warm-up ends at the first valid reading, or after 24 hours without one. A change that neither
shows is not detected. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Data gaps and sensor active are as defined in About This Report, Data. Time without data: the length of the period minus the time the readings
represent. Days with CGM data: the days of the period with any time represented by readings. Data gaps: the number of gaps that overlap the
period, and the longest of them at its full length, also where it extends beyond the period. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

Notes
GMI estimates A1C (glycated hemoglobin, a laboratory blood test) from mean CGM glucose.
In the data from which GMI was derived, the GMI and the laboratory A1C differed by 0,3 percentage points or more in 51% of 528 participants
and by 0,5 percentage points or more in 28% (Bergenstal et al., 2018, Table 3). This explains why the laboratory results in this section can differ
from the GMI shown beside them.
The ADA Standards of Care state that the comparability of A1C and mean CGM glucose depends on the number of days of CGM wear, the
timing of the A1C test relative to the CGM period, the accuracy of the meter and the CGM system, the lag between interstitial and venous
glucose, and factors that affect A1C or red blood cell turnover (American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes,
2026a, Correlation Between A1C and Blood Glucose Monitoring and Continuous Glucose Monitoring section, para. 2). This explains why a
laboratory result and the GMI of the 90 days before it can differ; the 90-day period is a GlucoCraft rule.
Each laboratory result is compared with the GMI of the 90 days ending on its date; GMI is shown only with at least 70% sensor active (the
condition of Battelino et al., 2019). This method is a GlucoCraft rule. CGM data are kept for 200 days, so a result whose 90 days begin earlier has
no CGM comparison. Difference: the laboratory A1C minus the GMI. Sensor active: data received in the 90 days ending on the date of the test. In
the Difference column, the first value is in percentage points and the second in mmol/mol. In mmol/mol, the GMI follows the GMI equation
(Bergenstal et al., 2018) and a laboratory A1C entered in percent the master equation (Hoelzel et al., 2004), so two values equal in percent can
differ by 1 mmol/mol.

calculated from the data received from the glucose sources and can differ from the reports of the CGM manufacturer's software.

Summary and full report: 
The 2019 international consensus describes a single-page report as of value and states that more detailed reports, for
example detailed daily reports, "should remain available for individualized review" (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data
Presentation section, para. 2). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care recommend a minimum of a single-page report,
such as the standardized CGM report and a weekly summary, and state that options for daily and weekly reports and raw data should be
available (American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026b, Recommendation 7.9). This explains why the
CGM Report has a summary and a full report with daily profiles, a daily summary and an hourly log, and why the readings can be exported as
comma-separated values (CSV). The summary contains the 14-day section (time in ranges, glucose metrics, the glucose profile and the daily
glucose profiles), the longer-term overview (30 days and longer), the weekly trend (90 days and 6 months), Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, the
comparison with the previous period (not in the 6-month report), Data Quality and Laboratory A1C. The full report adds Hypoglycemia Events
by Period, the daily glucose profiles of the whole period (30 days and longer), Daily Patterns, the Daily Summary, the Daily Log (one row per
day, one column per hour) and the Monthly Summary (every calendar month of the period). The two appendices are added to either form only
when chosen. Each section opens with a caption line that names its rule and source, shows its data and ends with Notes that explain them with
their sources.
Targets and assessments: 
GlucoCraft sets no targets or ranges and makes no assessments. Every target and range shown is either taken from
the cited published sources (consensus statements, studies and manufacturer documentation), each named as what it is — consensus: ranges
and targets (Battelino et al., 2019), tight range (Battelino et al., 2023), CV (Battelino et al., 2019; the study by Monnier et al., 2017); studies:
GMI (Bergenstal et al., 2018), GRI (Klonoff et al., 2023) — or set by the user in GlucoCraft's settings. Where GlucoCraft applies a rule of its own
(for example the length of a data gap, or the zone of a GRI value), it is labeled as a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft is designed to calculate and
display; it sends notifications, prints reports and saves PDF and CSV files only as chosen in its settings or requested by the user. Where colors
or the words met / not met appear, they are arithmetic comparisons with the cited target or the custom goal, not clinical assessments.
Data source. 
Test source.
Report period: 
full days ending at midnight before the report was created; the days and the night and day periods follow the time zone of the
system that created the report. The first section always shows the most recent 14 days, the recommended period (Battelino et al., 2019;
Bergenstal et al., 2013).
Period length: 
Among 257 people with type 1 diabetes, 14 days of CGM data estimated the 3-month time in range and mean glucose closely
(Riddlesworth et al., 2018). Time below range is less precise: among 329 people with type 1 diabetes with 90 days of CGM data, its error
roughly halved from 10 to 30 days of data and continued to decrease to 60 days (Cichosz et al., 2023).
Data: 
time without CGM data is excluded from all values. A data gap is an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three
reading intervals, whichever is longer, the reading interval being the median of the 10 intervals before the reading (the higher of the two middle
values; filled with the intervals after it at the start of the data; the usual interval of the source with fewer than 3). Each reading represents the time
until the next reading, so a shorter dropout counts in full (the values in between are not known); before a gap, only its own reading interval.
Sensor active is that time as a share of the period; the CGM system's own figure also counts readings not received for this report (for example
during delivery or network outages) and applies its own rules to short dropouts. Every percentage and every statistic weights each reading by the
time it represents. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Readings at the sensor's limit: 
a reading outside the CGM sensor's measurement range (shown in this report as LO or HI) has no value: it is
left out of the mean, the standard deviation, the CV, the GMI, the lowest and highest values and the glucose curves, and it is counted as very
low or very high in the time in ranges and in the events, where an event's lowest value can be LO. Its number and time are noted under the
statistics. No consensus document addresses such readings, and other software treats them differently: the report software of Abbott Diabetes
Care shows them at the limit (Abbott Diabetes Care, 2018, p. 7), so the values can differ from a manufacturer's report. This method is a
GlucoCraft rule.
Enough data: 
the values of a period (time in ranges, mean glucose, SD, CV, GMI, GRI, lowest and highest value, events and comparisons, also
those of a week or a day) are shown only when its sensor active is at least 70%, compared before rounding; otherwise the period's sensor active
is given and a dash (-) stands in place of its values. The 70% condition is published for 14-day periods (Battelino et al., 2019, Table 2); this
report applies it to periods of every length. The glucose profiles and the Daily Log show the readings received in any case. This method is a
GlucoCraft rule. A dash (-) also marks a value that does not exist for a period, such as GMI for fewer than 14 days.
Rounding: 
every value is calculated from the readings as stored and rounded once, where it is shown: percentages to one decimal (two where
one decimal would show a target's value that the value does not meet), glucose in mg/dL to whole numbers and in mmol/L to one decimal, with
halves rounded away from zero. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Durations: 
d, days; h, hours; min, minutes.
Not included: 
food intake, insulin, physical activity and device information are not part of the data.
A1C and GMI in mmol/mol: 
GMI in mmol/mol = 12,71 + 4,70587 × mean glucose in mmol/L (Bergenstal et al., 2018); laboratory A1C entered in
percent converted with the master equation of the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) and the
National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP), mmol/mol = 10,929 × (% − 2,15) (Hoelzel et al., 2004). The unit is chosen in the
settings.

Measures defined for research. 
This appendix shows measures that research publications define but that the clinical-care standards do not.
They are not part of the main report, they have no targets, and they are shown without color or comparison.
Definition. 
An event is a period in which sensor glucose stays above 13,9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL) for at least 120 minutes. It ends when glucose
has returned to 10,0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) or below for 15 minutes (Battelino et al., 2023, p. 48). This definition was made for counting events in
clinical trials: the 2023 international consensus statement lists the "extended hyperglycaemic event rate" as a secondary endpoint for clinical
studies (Battelino et al., 2023, p. 48). The same statement also describes extended hyperglycemia as 90 cumulative minutes above 13,9 mmol/L
(250 mg/dL) within a 120-minute period (Battelino et al., 2023, Table 4); this report uses the version that states both a start and an end.
No clinical-care standard. 
The clinical-care consensus describes high glucose by the time above 10,0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) and above 13,9
mmol/L (250 mg/dL) and sets targets for those times (Battelino et al., 2019); the ADA Standards of Care do the same (American Diabetes
Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026a, Table 6.2). Neither defines high-glucose events or a target for their number.
The 2023 definition exists only for research, so the count has no published target and no clinical interpretation.
Method 
(GlucoCraft rules where the source does not specify):
1.
The readings are the CGM values received for this report, in mg/dL; a HI reading counts at the sensor's upper limit (always above 250 mg/dL).
The limits in mmol/L are 13,9 and 10,0.
2.
Start: a run of consecutive readings, each above 250 mg/dL, becomes an event once the time it covers reaches 120 minutes. The time a run
covers is measured as in all statistics of this report: each reading counts until the next reading, or for its own reading interval before a data gap.
The event's start time is the time of the run's first reading.
3.
During the event, readings from 181 to 250 mg/dL do not end it.
4.
End: the event ends at the first reading of the first run of readings at or below 180 mg/dL that covers 15 minutes. Its duration is the time from its
start to that reading.
5.
Data gaps: a data gap (an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three reading intervals, whichever is longer) ends a
running event at the end of its last reading before the gap, which counts for its own reading interval. A run above 250 mg/dL interrupted by a gap
is an event only if it had already covered 120 minutes before the gap.
6.
Counting: each event is counted once, in the period and on the day in which it starts, also when it continues past midnight. The appendix
shows the number of events, their total duration and the longest event for the report period.
Limits. 
Only the readings received for this report are counted. An event during a gap in the data is not counted, or is counted shorter. The CGM
system's own data can contain readings that were not received for this report.

Other groups: 
The consensus also publishes different targets for some groups, such as older or high-risk adults and pregnancy (Battelino et al.,
2019, Tables 3 and 4). They are not included here. The results here are calculated with the ranges and targets for adults in general, not with the
ranges for these groups.
Names of the ranges: 
The 2019 international consensus names the glucose ranges of the standardized report "Very High" (level 2), "High" (level 1),
"Low" (level 1) and "Very Low" (level 2) (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data Presentation section, para. 1). This explains the range
names Very high, High, Low and Very low.
CV target: 
The 2019 international consensus sets the target for glycemic variability at a coefficient of variation (%CV) of 36% or less (Battelino et al.,
2019, Table 2), a value it takes from Monnier et al. (2017). The ADA Standards of Care list the same goal of 36% or less (American Diabetes
Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026a, Table 6.2). This explains the target in the CV row.
Metrics: 
mean glucose and the standard deviation (SD) are weighted by time, as described in About This Report (Data). Coefficient of variation (CV)
= SD ÷ mean glucose × 100 (Danne et al., 2017). Glucose management indicator (GMI) in percent = 3.31 + 0.02392 × mean glucose in mg/dL
(Bergenstal et al., 2018). Glycemia Risk Index (GRI) = 3.0 × very low + 2.4 × low + 1.6 × very high + 0.8 × high, each in percent of time, at most 100;
its hypoglycemia component is very low + 0.8 × low and its hyperglycemia component very high + 0.5 × high (Klonoff et al., 2023).
Glucose profile: 
The 2023 international consensus statement on CGM metrics for clinical trials describes four features of the graph of the glucose
profile: the target glucose range, the median line, the shaded 25th to 75th percentile band and the outer 5th to 95th percentile band (Battelino et al.,
2023, p. 49). This explains the lines and shaded bands of the glucose profile in the CGM Report. The cited sources do not describe the smoothing of
the profile; each 15-minute period is pooled with the two neighboring periods (45 minutes), and each reading counts once for every whole minute it
represents. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

The 2017 international consensus quantifies hypoglycemia both as the percentage of CGM values, or the minutes or hours, below a threshold and "as
the number of hypoglycemic events that occur over the given CGM reporting period" (Danne et al., 2017, Section 4, para. 13). This explains why this
section shows both the time below range and the number of events for the same period.
The 2017 international consensus states that "readings below the threshold for at least 15 min" are considered an event and that the event ends with
readings for 15 minutes at 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or higher (Danne et al., 2017, Section 4, para. 14). This explains how the level 1 and level 2 events
in the Hypoglycemia section are counted: an event is counted once its readings have been below its limit for 15 minutes, starts at its first reading
below the limit, and ends with 15 minutes at 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or higher.
Hypoglycemia event: 
An event is counted once its readings have been below its limit for 15 minutes, and it then starts at its first reading below the
limit. Its duration runs to the first reading of the 15 minutes at or above 70 mg/dL, or to the end of the time its last reading represents when a data
gap (as defined in About This Report, Data) follows or the readings end; it is counted in the period in which it starts, a level 2 event in that of its level
1 event. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. No consensus rule exists for these details.
Night and day: 
The 2017 international consensus reports the glucose metrics in three time blocks, sleep, wake and 24 hours, with default times from
midnight to 6 in the morning for sleep and from 6 in the morning to midnight for wake (Danne et al., 2017, Section 7). For clinical trials, the 2023
international consensus statement reports nocturnal data for 00:00 to 05:59 and daytime data for 06:00 to 23:59 (Battelino et al., 2023, Panel 2). This
explains the Night (12:00 AM–5:59 AM) and Day (6:00 AM–11:59 PM) columns of the Hypoglycemia table; the report's night is a clock period, not a
measure of sleep.
Chart: 
Each marker is one level 1 event, at its start time and lowest value; the marker size increases with the duration, up to 120 minutes. The darker
markers are events that contain a level 2 event (at least 15 consecutive minutes below 54 mg/dL; Danne et al., 2017, Section 4). The solid line marks
70 mg/dL and the broken line 54 mg/dL. A lowest value below the CGM sensor's measurement range (LO) is drawn at the sensor's lower limit.

This report: 
The CGM Report shows the standardized metrics and glucose profile recommended for the Ambulatory Glucose Profile (Battelino et al.,
2019; Bergenstal et al., 2013). GlucoCraft is not affiliated with or endorsed by the cited authors or any CGM manufacturer. The values are calculated
from the data received from the glucose sources and can differ from the reports of the CGM manufacturer's software.
Summary and full report: 
The 2019 international consensus describes a single-page report as of value and states that more detailed reports, for
example detailed daily reports, "should remain available for individualized review" (Battelino et al., 2019, Standardization of CGM Data Presentation
section, para. 2). The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care recommend a minimum of a single-page report, such as the
standardized CGM report and a weekly summary, and state that options for daily and weekly reports and raw data should be available (American
Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, 2026b, Recommendation 7.9). This explains why the CGM Report has a
summary and a full report with daily profiles, a daily summary and an hourly log, and why the readings can be exported as comma-separated values
(CSV). The summary contains the 14-day section (time in ranges, glucose metrics, the glucose profile and the daily glucose profiles), the
longer-term overview (30 days and longer), the weekly trend (90 days and 6 months), Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, the comparison with the
previous period (not in the 6-month report), Data Quality and Laboratory A1C. The full report adds Hypoglycemia Events by Period, the daily
glucose profiles of the whole period (30 days and longer), Daily Patterns, the Daily Summary, the Daily Log (one row per day, one column per hour)
and the Monthly Summary (every calendar month of the period). The two appendices are added to either form only when chosen. Each section
opens with a caption line that names its rule and source, shows its data and ends with Notes that explain them with their sources.

Targets and assessments: 
GlucoCraft sets no targets or ranges and makes no assessments. Every target and range shown is either taken from the
cited published sources (consensus statements, studies and manufacturer documentation), each named as what it is — consensus: ranges and
targets (Battelino et al., 2019), tight range (Battelino et al., 2023), CV (Battelino et al., 2019; the study by Monnier et al., 2017); studies: GMI
(Bergenstal et al., 2018), GRI (Klonoff et al., 2023) — or set by the user in GlucoCraft's settings. Where GlucoCraft applies a rule of its own (for
example the length of a data gap, or the zone of a GRI value), it is labeled as a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft is designed to calculate and display; it
sends notifications, prints reports and saves PDF and CSV files only as chosen in its settings or requested by the user. Where colors or the words
met / not met appear, they are arithmetic comparisons with the cited target or the custom goal, not clinical assessments.
Data source. 
Test source.
Report period: 
full days ending at midnight before the report was created; the days and the night and day periods follow the time zone of the system
that created the report. The first section always shows the most recent 14 days, the recommended period (Battelino et al., 2019; Bergenstal et al.,
2013).
Period length: 
Among 257 people with type 1 diabetes, 14 days of CGM data estimated the 3-month time in range and mean glucose closely
(Riddlesworth et al., 2018). Time below range is less precise: among 329 people with type 1 diabetes with 90 days of CGM data, its error roughly
halved from 10 to 30 days of data and continued to decrease to 60 days (Cichosz et al., 2023).
Data: 
time without CGM data is excluded from all values. A data gap is an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three
reading intervals, whichever is longer, the reading interval being the median of the 10 intervals before the reading (the higher of the two middle values;
filled with the intervals after it at the start of the data; the usual interval of the source with fewer than 3). Each reading represents the time until the
next reading, so a shorter dropout counts in full (the values in between are not known); before a gap, only its own reading interval. Sensor active is
that time as a share of the period; the CGM system's own figure also counts readings not received for this report (for example during delivery or
network outages) and applies its own rules to short dropouts. Every percentage and every statistic weights each reading by the time it represents.
This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Readings at the sensor's limit: 
a reading outside the CGM sensor's measurement range (shown in this report as LO or HI) has no value: it is left out
of the mean, the standard deviation, the CV, the GMI, the lowest and highest values and the glucose curves, and it is counted as very low or very
high in the time in ranges and in the events, where an event's lowest value can be LO. Its number and time are noted under the statistics. No
consensus document addresses such readings, and other software treats them differently: the report software of Abbott Diabetes Care shows them
at the limit (Abbott Diabetes Care, 2018, p. 7), so the values can differ from a manufacturer's report. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Enough data: 
the values of a period (time in ranges, mean glucose, SD, CV, GMI, GRI, lowest and highest value, events and comparisons, also
those of a week or a day) are shown only when its sensor active is at least 70%, compared before rounding; otherwise the period's sensor active is
given and a dash (-) stands in place of its values. The 70% condition is published for 14-day periods (Battelino et al., 2019, Table 2); this report
applies it to periods of every length. The glucose profiles and the Daily Log show the readings received in any case. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
A dash (-) also marks a value that does not exist for a period, such as GMI for fewer than 14 days.
Rounding: 
every value is calculated from the readings as stored and rounded once, where it is shown: percentages to one decimal (two where one
decimal would show a target's value that the value does not meet), glucose in mg/dL to whole numbers and in mmol/L to one decimal, with halves
rounded away from zero. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Durations: 
d, days; h, hours; min, minutes.
Not included: 
food intake, insulin, physical activity and device information are not part of the data.
A1C and GMI in mmol/mol: 
GMI in mmol/mol = 12.71 + 4.70587 × mean glucose in mmol/L (Bergenstal et al., 2018); laboratory A1C entered in
percent converted with the master equation of the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) and the National
